journey.what: The trip a web request takes: your browser looks up the address, connects securely, and a chain of servers answers.
journey.why: Every system you will ever design is a variation of this path. If you can walk it, you know where each tool (CDN, cache, database) fits and where things get slow.
use: Debugging a slow page: walk the path to find the slow step
Explaining a design: start at the browser and follow one request
Deciding where a cache or CDN would help
avoid: You do not need to memorise protocol details on day one. The order of the steps is what matters
journey.example: When Amazon loads, DNS finds the server, a CDN sends images from nearby, a load balancer picks an app server, and a database confirms your cart.
takeaways: A request flows browser, DNS, CDN, load balancer, app server, cache, database
Each step adds time and can fail
Connection setup is expensive, so reuse connections

net.what: The rules computers use to talk. TCP delivers everything in order, like registered mail. UDP just sends and hopes, like shouting across a room.
net.why: Choosing wrongly makes video calls laggy or file transfers corrupt. HTTP and TLS sit on top and make the web work securely.
use: TCP for web pages, databases and payments: anything that must arrive complete
UDP for live video, voice and games, where a late packet is useless
TLS whenever data crosses a network
avoid: Do not use UDP for data you cannot afford to lose unless you add your own checks
Do not open a new connection for every request. Reuse them
net.example: A Zoom call uses UDP-style transport so one lost packet does not freeze the picture. Your bank website uses TCP with TLS.
takeaways: TCP is reliable and ordered, UDP is fast and loose
A new connection costs several round trips

os.what: How a computer runs many programs at once (processes and threads) and stores data (memory, disks, object storage).
os.why: Most mysterious slowdowns are an operating system limit: too many threads, a full disk, or data that was not safely written yet.
use: Choosing threads or async I/O to handle many connections
Choosing object storage for big files and block storage for databases
Knowing when data is truly saved to disk
avoid: Do not create one thread per request at large scale
Do not treat RAID as a backup
os.example: A Node.js chat server handles thousands of users on a few threads with an event loop. Netflix keeps video files in object storage, not on server disks.
takeaways: Threads share memory, processes do not
Object storage is cheap and durable for files
RAID protects against a dead disk, not against mistakes

numbers.what: A feel for how fast and how reliable things are. Memory is quick, disks slower, networks slowest. And 99.9% uptime still means hours of downtime a year.
numbers.why: Designs are decisions about numbers. Without them you cannot tell whether a cache helps or whether an uptime goal is realistic.
use: Comparing options by latency (memory, SSD, network)
Judging speed by p99, not just the average
avoid: Do not trust averages alone. A few very slow requests hurt real users
numbers.example: Google watches the slowest 1% of searches, because a page that makes 100 calls will hit a slow one most of the time.
takeaways: Memory is about 1,000 times faster than SSD
Three 99.9% services in a row give about 99.7%
Look at p99 latency, not the average

estimate.what: Quick maths that turns '10 million users' into requests per second, storage and bandwidth.
estimate.why: The numbers choose the design. One database is fine for 1,000 requests a second but not for 100,000.
use: At the start of any design
Before choosing servers or a database
In interviews, to justify your choices
avoid: Do not chase exact numbers. The order of magnitude is enough
estimate.example: A URL shortener with 100 million new links a month needs only about 40 writes a second, so the heavy part is reads, which a cache handles.
takeaways: Daily requests divided by 86,400 gives requests per second
Count copies, indexes and backups when sizing storage

req.what: Deciding what to build, and which trade-offs you accept, before drawing anything: features, scale, speed, and what must never be wrong.
req.why: Most failed designs solve the wrong problem or promise perfection everywhere. Clear requirements prevent that.
use: At the start of every project or interview
When two teams disagree about what 'fast' or 'reliable' means
When choosing consistency over availability, or the reverse
avoid: Do not design for a billion users when you have a thousand
req.example: A bank balance must always be exactly right, while a like counter can be a little behind. Those two needs get different designs.
takeaways: Ask about scale, speed and what must never be wrong
Consistency versus availability is a choice per feature

lb.what: A traffic director that spreads requests across several identical servers and skips the ones that are down.
lb.why: One server is a single point of failure with a hard limit. Many servers behind a load balancer give more capacity and survive crashes.
use: You run more than one app server
You want deploys with no downtime
You route /api and /images to different server pools
avoid: Do not depend on sticky sessions. Keep servers stateless
Do not forget the load balancer itself needs a backup
lb.example: On Black Friday a shop runs 20 app servers behind a load balancer. When one crashes, customers never notice.
takeaways: It spreads load and hides failures

cache.what: A small, fast memory in front of a slow database that remembers recent answers.
cache.why: Reading from memory is thousands of times faster than a database, so a cache cuts waiting time and protects the database.
use: Data that is read far more than it is written
Expensive queries whose answers rarely change
avoid: Data that must always be perfectly fresh, like account balances
When the database is not actually the bottleneck
cache.example: Twitter keeps recent timelines in Redis, so opening the app does not hit the database for every tweet.
takeaways: Update or expire entries when data changes
Beware stampedes when a hot key expires

cdn.what: A network of servers around the world that keep copies of your images, scripts and videos close to each user.
cdn.why: Distance means delay, and your own servers carry less load.
avoid: Private or personalised responses, unless carefully marked
Content that changes every second
cdn.example: Netflix places cache boxes inside internet providers so a film streams from your own city.
takeaways: Use hashed file names so updates show immediately
Upload big files straight to object storage
Your origin only serves cache misses

queue.what: A line where work waits. The app drops a job in and answers at once, and workers pick it up and do it later.
queue.why: Slow tasks like email, video and reports do not slow the user down, spikes are absorbed, and failed jobs can retry.
use: Sending emails and notifications, processing uploads
Connecting services so they do not wait on each other
avoid: When the user needs the result right now
If your workers cannot safely handle the same job twice
queue.example: When you upload a video to YouTube it is queued, then workers convert it into many sizes.
takeaways: It decouples the sender from the worker
Delivery is usually at least once, so handle duplicates
A dead-letter queue holds jobs that keep failing

db.what: Where your data lives for good. The main choices are relational (tables and joins), key-value, document and search stores.
db.why: The wrong store makes simple things hard. Matching the store to how you read and write saves months of pain.
use: Relational for orders and payments, anything needing transactions
Key-value for sessions and fast lookups
A search engine for text search
avoid: Do not pick NoSQL just because it sounds scalable
Do not use the database as a queue or a cache
db.example: Most shops use PostgreSQL for orders, Redis for sessions and Elasticsearch for product search.
takeaways: Add a specialised store only for a named need

shard.what: Splitting one big database into smaller pieces (shards), each holding part of the data. Indexes help you find rows quickly inside each piece.
shard.why: One machine eventually cannot hold or write all the data. Indexes speed up reads on one machine, and shards spread the load across many.
use: Add indexes first when queries are slow
Shard when one database cannot keep up with writes or size
Use consistent hashing so adding a shard moves little data
avoid: Do not shard early. It makes joins and transactions much harder
shard.example: Instagram spreads its users across many database shards by user ID.
takeaways: A good shard key spreads load evenly
Consistent hashing moves few keys when you add a node

repl.what: Keeping copies of your database on other machines, so you have backups and extra servers to read from.
repl.why: A copy survives a failure and shares the read traffic, but copies can lag behind the original.
use: Backups and reporting without slowing the main database
avoid: Reading right after a write from a lagging copy without handling it
repl.example: A news site writes to one primary database and serves readers from several replicas.
takeaways: The leader takes writes and followers serve reads
Failover needs care so you never get two leaders

engines.what: How a database stores bytes on disk. B-trees update data in place. LSM-trees write new files quickly and tidy up later.
engines.why: It explains why some databases are great at reads and others cope with enormous write volumes.
use: B-tree databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) for general use
LSM databases (Cassandra, RocksDB) for very heavy writes
avoid: You do not need this until you choose or tune a database
engines.example: Cassandra uses LSM-trees to absorb millions of sensor writes a second.
takeaways: Compaction is the hidden cost of LSM

tx.what: A transaction groups several changes so they all happen or none do. Isolation levels decide what other users can see meanwhile.
tx.why: Without them, two people paying at the same moment can corrupt balances.
use: Anything where a half-finished update would be harmful
avoid: Very long transactions, which block other users
Assuming the default isolation level is the strictest one
tx.example: Transferring money subtracts from one account and adds to another in a single transaction.
takeaways: Read-modify-write in app code can lose updates

model.what: Deciding how to shape your data: store each fact once (normalised) or copy it to where it is read (denormalised).
model.why: A good shape makes your most common questions fast and simple to answer.
use: Denormalise for hot read paths or in document stores
avoid: Duplicating data without a plan to keep the copies in sync
model.example: A product page that always shows its five images stores them inside the product document.
takeaways: Embed small data that is read together

serial.what: The format used to turn data into bytes for sending or storing. JSON is readable text. Protobuf and Avro are compact binary.
serial.why: The format affects speed, size, and whether old and new software can still talk to each other.
avoid: Removing or renaming fields in a single release
serial.example: Google uses Protobuf inside its systems for fast, typed calls between services.
takeaways: Add fields, never remove them or reuse their numbers
Send big numbers as strings in JSON

datatypes.what: A tour of specialised databases: time-series, wide-column, search, graph and vector stores.
datatypes.why: Each is built for one pattern. Using the right one avoids painful workarounds.
avoid: Making a search index your only copy of the data
datatypes.example: 'Songs like this one' features use vector search over embeddings.
takeaways: Match the store to the question
Keep one source of truth, the others derived
Keep stores in sync with events

cap.what: When the network splits, a system must choose: stay correct (refuse some requests) or stay available (answer, possibly with old data).
cap.why: It tells you what to expect from every database, and how to design around it.
use: Choose consistency for money and bookings
Choose availability for carts and feeds
avoid: Believing you can have everything at once
cap.example: Cassandra keeps answering during a network split. etcd refuses writes unless it has a majority.
takeaways: Speed versus freshness matters even without splits

consensus.what: How a group of machines agree on a single answer, such as who the leader is, even when some of them fail.
consensus.why: Locks, leader election and shared configuration all need agreement that survives failures.
use: Use etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul for coordination
Understand Raft when you run clusters
avoid: Do not write your own consensus system
consensus.example: Kubernetes keeps its cluster state in etcd, which uses Raft.
takeaways: It needs a majority of nodes
Losing the majority stops writes safely

clocks.what: Why computers disagree about the time, and how to order events without trusting clocks.
clocks.why: Using timestamps to decide a winner can silently lose data.
use: Use logical or vector clocks to order events
Use a monotonic clock to measure durations
avoid: Last-write-wins on wall-clock time for important data
clocks.example: Two phones edit a note offline. Vector clocks reveal the edits were concurrent, so they can be merged instead of one being lost.
takeaways: Lamport clocks give a consistent order

api.what: The contract your service offers: URLs, methods, status codes, and safe ways to retry.
api.why: A good API survives retries, growth and many different callers.
avoid: Offset pagination on data that changes while people page through it
api.example: Stripe asks for an idempotency key so a retried payment is never charged twice.

apistyles.what: Three ways to offer an API: REST (simple web resources), GraphQL (the client asks for exactly the fields it needs), and gRPC (fast binary calls).
apistyles.why: Each one suits a different kind of caller.
use: REST for public and partner APIs
avoid: Opening GraphQL without query depth limits
apistyles.example: GitHub offers both a REST and a GraphQL API.
takeaways: gRPC needs a proxy for browsers

gateway.what: A front door for many services that handles login, routing and limits. Also the tricks for finding services and for moving away from an old monolith.
gateway.why: Clients should not need to know about dozens of separate services.
use: Gradually replacing an old system (strangler fig)
avoid: Putting business logic inside the gateway
gateway.example: Netflix's gateway sends each device request to the right backend services.
takeaways: Migrate one path at a time

micro.what: Splitting an app into small services that can be built and deployed independently.
micro.why: Big teams move faster and parts can scale separately.
use: Parts with very different scaling needs
avoid: Small teams or brand-new products
Without good monitoring in place
micro.example: Amazon splits cart, orders, payments and search into separate services.
takeaways: Use sagas instead of shared transactions

eventdriven.what: Services announce 'something happened' and others react, instead of calling each other directly.
eventdriven.why: It keeps teams loosely coupled and absorbs spikes.
use: An order placed triggers email, stock and analytics
avoid: When you need an immediate answer
If your handlers cannot cope with duplicates
eventdriven.example: Uber publishes trip events that many other systems consume.

resil.what: Ways to keep working when parts fail: timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers and fallbacks.
resil.why: Failures spread. These patterns stop one slow service from taking everything down.
avoid: Retrying without jitter
Retrying actions that are not safe to repeat
resil.example: Netflix shows a generic list when personalised recommendations are down.

ratelimiter.what: A limiter that allows only a set number of requests over a period of time.
ratelimiter.why: It protects you from abuse and from runaway clients.
avoid: Limiting only by IP address behind shared networks
ratelimiter.example: GitHub limits how many API calls each user can make per hour.
takeaways: A token bucket allows short bursts
Share counters in Redis across servers

observe.what: Seeing inside a running system through logs (what happened), metrics (how much) and traces (where the time went).
observe.why: You cannot fix what you cannot see.
avoid: Alerting on every single metric
Logging personal data
observe.example: Engineers follow one request through five services using a trace.
takeaways: Put a request ID on every log line

slo.what: Turning 'reliable' into numbers: an SLI is what you measure, an SLO is the target, an SLA is the promise to customers, and the error budget is what you may spend.
slo.why: It lets teams balance shipping new features against keeping things stable.
avoid: Targets stricter than your users actually need
slo.example: A 99.9% target over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of failure.
takeaways: The error budget guides release speed
Alert on how fast the budget burns

chaos.what: Breaking things on purpose, safely, to find weaknesses before real failures do. Also how to run an incident calmly.
chaos.why: Systems fail in surprising ways, and it is better to find out on your terms.
use: Mature systems that already have monitoring
avoid: Experiments with no way to stop them
chaos.example: Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly shuts down servers to prove the service survives.
takeaways: Define what normal looks like first

auth.what: Proving who someone is (authentication), checking what they may do (authorisation), and defending against common web attacks.
auth.why: Most breaches come from a skipped check, not from clever hacking.
avoid: Rolling your own cryptography
Storing plain-text passwords
auth.example: Changing an ID in a URL to see someone else's invoice (IDOR) is a classic bug.

netsec.what: Keeping data encrypted and networks small: TLS in transit, encryption at rest, private subnets and least privilege.
netsec.why: It limits the damage of any single mistake.
avoid: Public databases
Wildcard permissions
netsec.example: Many real data leaks are simply a storage bucket left open to the internet.
takeaways: Keep secrets in a secrets manager

containers.what: Packaging an app with everything it needs (Docker), and letting Kubernetes run many copies and keep them healthy.
containers.why: The same package runs identically on a laptop and in production.
avoid: A tiny app on one server
Without resource limits
containers.example: A team runs 50 services as containers on Kubernetes.
takeaways: Pin image versions, never use latest

iac.what: Describing servers and networks in files (Terraform) so changes can be reviewed and recreated.
iac.why: Clicking around a cloud console cannot be reviewed or repeated.
use: Several environments such as staging and production
avoid: Applying without reading the plan
Making hand edits in the console
iac.example: A team runs terraform plan in every pull request, so infrastructure changes get reviewed like code.

serverless.what: Running code without managing servers. You pay per call and the platform scales it for you.
serverless.why: There are no servers to maintain and cost follows usage.
avoid: Long-running jobs
Latency-critical paths that cannot tolerate cold starts
serverless.example: Resizing a photo after upload with AWS Lambda.
takeaways: Many parallel functions can overwhelm a database

deploy.what: Shipping new versions safely: automated tests, staged releases, rollbacks and careful database changes.
deploy.why: Most outages follow a change, so safe releases prevent most outages.
avoid: Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it
deploy.example: A canary release sends a new version to 2% of users first.
takeaways: Watch the dashboards after a release

scale.what: The order in which to add building blocks as real traffic grows.
scale.why: It stops you building too little, or far too much.
avoid: Sharding early
scale.example: Many products serve millions of users with just a cache and a few read replicas.
takeaways: Keep servers stateless from day one

streaming.what: A replayable log of events (Kafka) that many programs read at their own pace.
streaming.why: It powers real-time pipelines and keeps event history.
avoid: Small, simple task queues
streaming.example: LinkedIn created Kafka to move activity data between its systems.

batch.what: Crunching huge datasets in bulk (MapReduce, Spark) and storing them in warehouses for analysis.
batch.why: Questions about the whole history of your data need a different kind of system from your live database.
avoid: Running analytics on your live production database
batch.example: A nightly job totals the day's revenue for every shop.

solid.what: Five habits for writing classes that stay easy to change.
solid.why: Code changes constantly, and these habits keep each change small and safe.
use: When one change keeps breaking unrelated things
avoid: Over-abstracting small scripts
solid.example: Adding a new discount type by adding a class instead of editing a giant if/else.
takeaways: Each class has one reason to change
Extend by adding code, not editing

oop.what: Turning requirements into classes, methods and relationships.
oop.why: A clear model is easy to explain, test and extend.
avoid: Deep inheritance trees
oop.example: A parking lot has Vehicle, Spot and Ticket classes.
takeaways: Nouns become classes, verbs become methods

patterns.what: Named, proven solutions to common design problems.
patterns.why: They give teams a shared vocabulary.
use: State for behaviour that depends on state
avoid: Adding a pattern just to look clever
patterns.example: A vending machine uses the State pattern for idle, has-money and dispensing.
takeaways: Start plain, add a pattern when change hurts
Strategy, Observer and State cover most cases
Name the pattern when you use it

conc.what: Handling several things at once without corrupting shared data.
conc.why: Race conditions cause rare, hard-to-reproduce bugs.
avoid: Holding a lock while waiting on the network
conc.example: Two people try to book the last seat at the same moment.
takeaways: Take locks in the same order to avoid deadlock
Across servers, use a database atomic update

parking.what: A classic design exercise: park and release vehicles and charge fees.
parking.why: It practises modelling and concurrency in one small problem.
avoid: Skipping the concurrent-allocation edge case
parking.example: Two cars arriving at two gates must never get the same spot.
takeaways: Handle lost tickets and a full lot

lru.what: A cache that throws out the least recently used item first, built from a hash map and a linked list.
lru.why: Memory is limited, so something must be evicted.
avoid: A cache with no size limit
lru.example: Your browser keeps recent pages and drops the oldest.
takeaways: Hash map plus doubly linked list gives O(1)
Updating an existing key must not grow the cache

urlshort.what: A service that turns a long web address into a short one and redirects visitors.
urlshort.why: A great first full design: tiny writes, huge reads, and a few classic problems.
avoid: Sequential codes that let anyone guess other people's links
Accepting target URLs without any abuse or phishing checks

chat.what: A real-time messaging system with delivery states, groups and offline users.
chat.why: It shows how persistent connections, ordering and fan-out work.
avoid: Assuming a message arrives once, with no IDs or acknowledgements
Pushing one message to every member of a huge group at once
chat.example: WhatsApp keeps hundreds of millions of connections open.
takeaways: Use WebSockets and a session router
Use client message IDs to dedupe
Fan out large groups through a queue

feed.what: A personalised timeline of posts from people you follow.
feed.why: It teaches the trade-off between doing work when posting versus when reading.
avoid: Pushing a celebrity's post into millions of feeds on write
Offset pagination on a feed that changes every second
feed.example: Twitter pushes tweets to followers' timelines, except for huge accounts.
takeaways: Push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities

ecommerce.what: An online store: catalogue, cart, orders and payments.
ecommerce.why: It combines reads, careful writes and external services in one design.
avoid: Charging a card with no idempotency key on retries
Holding stock forever for abandoned carts
ecommerce.example: Amazon decouples order placement from payment processing with queues.
takeaways: Return an order ID fast, process payment asynchronously
Use idempotency keys and a circuit breaker

netflix.what: A video streaming service: upload, encode into many sizes, store and deliver from the edge.
netflix.why: It shows why bandwidth, caches and CDNs dominate such a design.
avoid: Serving popular titles straight from one origin
Encoding a single bitrate for every network
netflix.example: Netflix Open Connect boxes sit inside internet providers.
takeaways: Adaptive streaming adjusts to the viewer's network

kvstore.what: A key-value database like Dynamo: partitioned, replicated and tolerant of failures.
kvstore.why: It shows how large databases are really built.
avoid: Workloads that need joins or multi-row transactions
Last-write-wins on clocks when losing a write matters
kvstore.example: Amazon's Dynamo inspired Cassandra and DynamoDB.
takeaways: Quorums (R plus W greater than N) give fresh reads
Repair with hinted handoff and Merkle trees

clickstream.what: A pipeline that collects millions of click events and turns them into live and historical numbers.
clickstream.why: It combines streaming, batch and storage ideas.
avoid: Running heavy analytics on the production database
Counting events without handling late or duplicate ones
clickstream.example: A website counts page views per minute while keeping raw events for later.
takeaways: Use event time and watermarks for late events
Give each event a unique ID to dedupe

interview.what: A reusable routine for design interviews, plus the problems mapped to the lessons that teach them.
interview.why: A calm structure stops you jumping to boxes before you understand the problem.
avoid: Listing technologies without reasons
interview.example: Start with questions about users and scale, then estimate, then draw.

mvp.what: The smallest version of a product that proves the idea.
mvp.why: It gets real feedback early and avoids building things nobody wants.
use: When time and people are limited
avoid: Building infrastructure before you have users
mvp.example: Dropbox started as a simple demo video before the full product.

backend.what: How to organise server code: routes, services and repositories, with validation, configuration and migrations.
backend.why: Clean layers make code easy to test and change.
avoid: Putting business logic inside route handlers
backend.example: A FastAPI app with routers, services and a database layer.
takeaways: Paginate lists and avoid N+1 queries

projects.what: Hands-on projects that turn reading into skill.
projects.why: Running a system teaches things reading cannot.
use: After each topic, whenever you are ready
avoid: Trying to do everything at once
projects.example: Build a small service, load test it, then break it on purpose.
takeaways: Pick one project at a time

search.what: A separate system that keeps a word-to-documents map, so it can find and rank matches in milliseconds.
search.why: Scanning a database for words is slow and cannot rank results or forgive typos.
use: Ranking by relevance, filters and facets
avoid: As your only source of truth
Lookups by id that a normal database answers better
search.example: A shop's search box uses Elasticsearch to find products by their words, and a trie of popular queries for the suggestion drop-down.
takeaways: The index is a copy that lags the database
Index and query must use the same analyzer
Autocomplete is its own faster structure

geo.what: A way to find the closest places or people by cutting the map into cells and only looking in the right few.
geo.why: Comparing your position with millions of points is far too slow.
avoid: A handful of places you can scan directly
Ranking by distance alone when roads matter
geo.example: A ride app keeps each driver's position in memory under a map cell, so finding the nearest ones means reading a handful of cells.
takeaways: Turn 2D space into cell ids an index can use
Live positions belong in memory, not on disk

notify.what: A service that decides who should be told what, then sends push, SMS or email through outside providers.
notify.why: Sending directly from your app is slow, unreliable and easy to overdo.
use: Campaigns sent to millions of users
avoid: Urgent codes in the same queue as campaigns
Sending without checking preferences
notify.example: A shop publishes an 'order shipped' event, and the notification service sends a push, with email as a fallback.
takeaways: One queue and worker per channel
Idempotency key plus retries with backoff

dr.what: A plan and a set of copies that let your system keep working, or come back quickly, after losing a whole data centre or region.
dr.why: Entire regions do fail, and without a plan you lose data and hours of revenue.
use: Systems where downtime costs real money
Services with legal or contractual uptime promises
avoid: Paying for active-active when a short outage is acceptable
Backups you have never tested
dr.example: A bank replicates its database to a second region and rehearses a switch-over every quarter.
takeaways: Agree RPO and RTO with the business first
Replication lag is your data loss
